summary: Mount Utsayantha tower near Stamford NY: steel tower built 1934, fire lookout until 1989, village-owned, restored 2004-05, NHLR-registered 2015; open to climb.

facts.design: 59-foot-3-inch steel International Derrick fire tower (the Register gives 60 feet and an Aermotor)

staffing.status: not staffed at the October 2017 Register visit; volunteer steward program planned for 2026

access.note: The Register says it is maintained and open to the public to climb. Reached by a seasonal, narrow road from Mountain Road in Stamford (FFLA February 2026).

visit.trail_note: Drive up Mountain Road, which is seasonal and narrow; the FFLA suggests parking at the top, where the shoulder is wide, and walking the rest. The park at the base has picnic tables, bbq grills, benches, and bathroom facilities.

events.note: First tower on the summit, built as a tourist attraction; later blown over in 1892, 1895, 1901 and 1916 (FFLA February 2026, citing Podskoch)
Stamford citizen buys 20 acres, builds a four-story observation house, deeds the property to the town as a park
State steel fire tower built; the Register credits the NY Dept. of Conservation, the FFLA and Wikipedia credit Civilian Conservation Corps crews
First year of operation: 450 visitors and 13 fires reported (FFLA February 2026)
1953 Oneonta Star report: observers to report to the Albany Filter Center; James Davies of Stamford at the summit
Fire lookout operations ceased at the end of the 1989 season and the tower was decommissioned
Village bought the tower from the state; FFLA $200 restoration grant (only tower to receive one that year); AmeriCorps and FFLA members painted it in October 2004
Restoration begun in 2004 completed in July 2005 (Wikipedia)
FFLA steward program begins at Mt. Utsayantha

notes_for_editor: Core dates (1934 build, 1989 end of service, village ownership, 2004-05 restoration, 2015 registration) agree across the Register, the FFLA and Wikipedia. Conflicts are recorded in resolved_conflicts. The 1933 newspaper report on Forest Lookouts names a 60-foot steel tower to be completed in September 1933, so the 1934 build year is the consensus, not a certainty. The Register's visit report is dated October 21, 2017 (Laurie Rankin); its 'needs paint' and 'good overall condition' lines come from that visit, so they are nine years old as of 2026. The brief's agency (NYSDEC) is corrected to village ownership. No photo was added: the Register's photo is credited to Laurie Rankin (Oct 2017) and no image URL was retrieved. The brief's andyarthur.org page for the summit (p/216687) was not read.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: A 1933 newspaper report said construction would be completed in September 1933. The Register, the FFLA and Wikipedia all give 1934. The facts use 1934.
The Register gives a 60-foot Aermotor tower. The FFLA and Wikipedia give 59 ft 3 in (18.06 m), an International Derrick. The facts use the 59 ft 3 in figure and the story does not name a maker.
The Register credits the NY Dept. of Conservation; the FFLA and Wikipedia credit Civilian Conservation Corps crews. These are compatible: the state built the tower with CCC labour.

The Register lists NYSDEC as administering agency and the village as owner of the tower and park. The 2004 FFLA report says the village bought the tower from the state. The facts record the village as owner.
